A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weight-generative fine-tuning work, renamed from GIFT to WeGeFT. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V4 reports original GIFT fine-tuning results for reasoning, instruction following, GLUE, and visual recognition, together with generator and layer-selection ablations.

after.justification: V5 reports original WeGeFT results, including MetaMathQA and code generation, and new parameter-sharing, rank, and precision experiments.

M1.justification: The central shared two-linear-layer generator is retained. V5 introduces WeGeFT-Sep with separate learned matrices for individual layers (Section 3.1), while v4's within-block QKV/UG sharing variant is no longer presented. These revise the adaptation variants within the existing framework.

E1.justification: V5 adds MetaMathQA training and Code-Feedback/HumanEval code generation, replaces the Alpaca52k/UltraFeedback/Alpaca-Eval instruction-following pipeline with WizardLM/MT-Bench, and removes the six reported GLUE tasks. Math10k, Commonsense170k, FGVC, and VTAB remain covered.

E2.justification: Math10k adds DoRA, VB-LoRA, and FacT-TT/TK while removing PrefT and AdapterS/P. Commonsense170k adds VB-LoRA, and VTAB adds FacT variants. New comparisons include PiSSA, rsLoRA, LoRA+, AdaLoRA, and LoRA-GA. Table 9's new comparator is simplified Shared LoRA, described as an alternative formulation inspired by Tied-LoRA.

E3.justification: Math10k adds Llama 2 and rank-2 LoRA/DoRA budget controls. The shared input-side variant's stated scaling factor and warmup ratio change from 64 and 0.06 to 128 and 0.1 (v4 Table 10; v5 Table 12). Instruction evaluation changes from pairwise win rates with greedy decoding to first-turn ratings with sampling. V5 also introduces HumanEval Pass@1 and precision-comparison protocols.

E4.justification: V5 adds the Shared LoRA weight-awareness control (Section 5.2), VeRA rank sensitivity (Appendix A), and mixed-precision/rank analysis (Appendix B). It removes v4's projection-versus-Query/Value ablation and generation case studies. The nonlinear-generator ablation and visual token-clustering examples are retained.

E5.justification: Three-seed averaging for Math10k and commonsense reasoning is unchanged. V4 reports two-run instruction-following averages and five-seed GLUE medians; v5 drops those experiments and reports three-run means with ± values for MetaMathQA, MT-Bench, and HumanEval. This changes reporting across different experiments, without establishing increased replication of retained evaluations. The ± quantities are not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: For LLaMA-1 commonsense reasoning, the shared input-side comparison changes from GIFT 82.2 versus LoRA 74.7 (v4 Table 2) to WeGeFT 82.6 versus LoRA 83.0 (v5 Table 3), with revised comparison settings. New results include 54.89±0.92 GSM8k accuracy after MetaMathQA training and 19.39±0.68 HumanEval Pass@1. GLUE and Alpaca-Eval results disappear; FGVC accuracies remain identical, and retained VTAB accuracies are rounded.

T1.justification: V5 Equation 8 adds the transpose missing from v4 Equation 9's equivalent input-activation mapping, although its preceding weight-product expression conflicts with v5 Equation 3. The gradient comparison from v4 Section 2.3 is largely restated using sums over layers in v5 Appendix C; it is not a newly added proof.

C1.justification: V4's headline claims of best baseline performance, approximately 15-fold parameter savings, and beating GPT-3.5 are replaced by claims centered on combined parameter, representation, compute, and memory efficiency with matching or better performance. V5 foregrounds weight awareness and scalability, adds code generation to the claimed applications, and drops the language-understanding contribution. Weight generation and the PEFT/ReFT bridge remain central.

C2.justification: V5 adds data-quality and precision interpretations, explains ReFT resource differences through unequal gradient checkpointing, and acknowledges DoRA's advantage on LLaMA-1 and Llama 2 commonsense experiments. It replaces v4's distribution-shift conjecture about nonlinear generators with optimization and knowledge-preservation explanations, explicitly limits their evaluation to small models, and adds heuristic convergence/stability interpretations in Appendix C.

D1.justification: V5 newly documents weight dropout and precision/checkpointing details, and provides training and decoding settings for MetaMathQA, WizardLM, and Code-Feedback (Tables 13, 15, and 16). It replaces Math10k/commonsense search grids with selected values and omits earlier VeRA grids and some VTAB split/search details. These substantially revise the available reproducibility information; newly disclosed dropout does not establish whether it was absent from v4's implementation.

R1.justification: V4 presents parameter sharing as a gap in the discussed methods. V5 positions its novelty against Tied-LoRA and VB-LoRA, expands discussion of the previously cited FacT, and emphasizes weight-aware sharing. It also adds MEND, recent LoRA variants, and new benchmark references while removing GLUE/Alpaca-related citations. This substantively revises research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten, and GIFT is renamed WeGeFT. Related work moves before the approach, arithmetic reasoning becomes the first experiment, gradient analysis moves to Appendix C, and earlier introductory interpretation becomes a separate remarks section. Terminology and variant notation are substantially simplified.

P2.justification: V5 adopts a two-column main text and bibliography, separates and redraws the opening architecture/performance displays, and adds a GPU-memory/training-time figure. Reasoning tables gain resource columns, new experimental tables appear, and VTAB moves into the main text. Vision tables lose memory columns. Existing token-clustering images are retained and relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: V5 substantially strengthens testing of the central efficiency and weight-awareness claims through comparisons run in a common codebase, parameter-budget controls, a direct Shared LoRA ablation, and rank/precision/resource analyses (Table 2, Table 9, Appendices A and B). Reporting cases where LoRA or DoRA wins also improves the qualification of performance claims. Removing GLUE and the projection-layer ablation narrows supporting evidence, and mathematical inconsistencies and heuristic optimization claims remain, but the central empirical argument becomes substantially better supported and easier to assess.
